 After his win over Jan-Lennard Struff at the Rolex Paris Masters, Casper Ruud delivered a clear-eyed analysis of modern tennis. According to the Norwegian, players now defend topspin far better and take the initiative much earlier.
 Casper Ruud during the third round of the 2026 Australian Open. © MARTIN KEEP AFP Arthur Millot 06/11/2026, 09:34 2 min to read Follow us ATP Masters 1000 Paris Ruud Casper Ruud offered an interesting reflection on the evolution of modern tennis.
 Having qualified for the quarterfinals of the Rolex Paris Masters after his win over Jan-Lennard Struff, the Norwegian explained why he believes long rallies and extended duels are becoming less frequent these days.
 Remove ads Appearing on Tennis Channel, the former world No. 2 also discussed the adjustments he must make to his game to stay competitive against the new generation.
 "Players handle topspin much better now"
 "The hardest part of the evolution of my game is that most players today play at a very high tempo, both on the forehand and the backhand.
 For my part, I like to build points and play with a lot of topspin, a bit like Nadal and Thiem used to do.
 They were my idols growing up. But I've had to accept that players are now far better at defending against topspin balls.
 There will be fewer long rallies in modern tennis, because everyone serves well, returns well, and attacks as soon as an opening appears.
 For my part, I haven't always dared to take risks and hit big only when the opportunity presented itself.
 I've sometimes been too passive, because my game was more about gradually wearing the opponent down, forcing errors, or waiting for an easier ball to attack.
 But today, you see players who hit extremely hard in almost every situation, and I'm also trying to adopt that approach more. It's a constant challenge, and it probably will be until the end of my career."
 A more aggressive game to return to the top
 This desire to take more initiative is already showing on the court. Against Jan-Lennard Struff, Casper Ruud was notably able to rely on the quality of his return of serve to gain the upper hand over the German.
 "My return of serve is working well on this fast surface, and I think that has a lot to do with footwork quality and reactivity.
 Against Struff, you obviously have to be careful with his serve and his ability to come to the net. But when I broke him in the first set, I hit some very good returns, which proved decisive.
 In the past, I sometimes struggled against players who serve and volley, because I stood too far behind the baseline. My returns were too high and too floaty, which allowed them to finish at the net.
 But today, I read his serve very well. I think that forced him to stay further back in the second set, and I was able to take advantage of it," he concluded.
